personalEssay.prompt: Reflect on something that someone has done for you that has made you happy or thankful in a surprising way. How has this gratitude affected or motivated you?
personalEssay.text:
Ten minutes before my arangetram, my ankle bells broke.

If you don't know Bharatanatyam, an arangetram is a solo debut, about three hours long, that you train for over years. It's kind of like a graduation, a recital, and a wedding all at once. My family had rented a school auditorium in Edison, my teacher had flown in her nattuvanar, and my relatives had come from Chennai, Dallas, and Toronto. My salangai, the strings of brass bells I tie around my ankles, had been my teacher's when she was young, and she had given them to me the year I turned twelve.

When I pulled the left one tight backstage, the cord snapped. Bells everywhere. One rolled under a drum case.

I want to say I stayed calm. I did not. I sat on the floor in my costume and full makeup and tried very hard not to cry, because if I cried, the eyeliner would run and then I would really have to cry. My mom ran to find my teacher. My dad ran to find nobody in particular. And my paati, my grandmother, who is seventy-nine and was supposed to be sitting in the front row, came backstage, looked at the mess, and sat down on the floor next to me.

My paati speaks Tamil and about forty words of English. She doesn't drive. She doesn't really understand what I do at Science Olympiad, even though she asks about it every week. For most of my life I thought of her as someone I take care of: I read her medicine labels, I set up video calls with her sisters, I explain the plots of Netflix shows. I did not think of her as someone who could fix anything in an emergency.

She opened her purse. From somewhere inside it, next to the cough drops and a small steel tiffin of murukku, she pulled out a needle that was already threaded with thick black thread. She said, "Priyu, kaal kudu." Give me your foot. And then, sitting on a gym-floor stage in New Jersey, she re-strung my bells one by one, faster than I have ever seen her do anything, while my teacher held the ones we'd found and counted them out loud.

It took six minutes. We started on time.

Afterward I asked her why she had a threaded needle in her purse. She shrugged and said she always carried one, since she was a girl in Madurai, in case something tore. She had been carrying it my whole life and I had never known.

I think about that needle a lot. Not because it saved the performance, although it did, but because of what it showed me about how I'd been seeing her. I'd been so focused on the things my paati couldn't do in America, the language, the driving, the technology, that I'd stopped noticing what she'd been quietly ready to do the entire time.

It changed how I volunteer at the hospital, too. On the pediatric floor there are a lot of grandparents sitting in the corners of rooms, often not speaking much English, while parents talk to doctors. I used to just smile at them and restock the gloves. Now I ask them questions, even with gestures, even badly. Last month a grandmother showed me how she'd been folding paper cranes for her grandson's IV pole. She had made forty-two.

My paati still doesn't totally get Science Olympiad. But this year, when I left for the regional tournament, she pressed something into my hand and told me to keep it in my bag. It was a needle, already threaded.

supplements.prompt: Please explain why you wish to study in the academic areas you selected.
supplements.text:
I selected Biochemistry and Cell Biology because the parts of science I love most are the parts too small to see. In Disease Detectives I learned to trace an outbreak backward through a population. At the Waksman Institute last summer I traced a gene the same way, from a band on a gel back to a sequence and a function, and it felt like the same kind of detective work at a different scale.

I'm also drawn to Rice's Global Health Technologies minor, because I don't want to understand disease only in a lab. Volunteering on a pediatric floor showed me that the hardest part of medicine is often communication, especially with families who don't speak English. I want to study the molecules and also the people.
